stem.text: Alanine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)COOH, is an amino acid that contains a chiral centre.
Different synthetic routes to produce alanine can lead to the formation of an optically active sample or a racemic mixture.
Describe what is meant by optically active.

guidance: A (a substance able to) rotate plane of (plane) polarised light.
I rotating an amino acid instead of plane of polarised light.

points.text: (a substance able to) rotate plane polarised light

explanation.text: An optically active substance rotates the plane of plane-polarised light that passes through it. A sample is optically active when it contains a chiral compound and the two enantiomers are not present in equal amounts, for example a single enantiomer of alanine.

reasoningChain: State the effect: it rotates the plane of plane-polarised light.

inferredMistakes.text: Saying that the substance (or the amino acid) itself rotates, rather than the plane of polarised light, which the MS ignores.
Defining a chiral centre instead of describing optical activity.

stem.text: Describe what is meant by racemic mixture.

points.text:
(a mixture containing) equal amounts / proportions / concentrations
and
of optical isomers / enantiomers / stereoisomers

explanation.text: A racemic mixture contains the two enantiomers (optical isomers) in equal amounts. Each enantiomer rotates plane-polarised light by the same angle in opposite directions, so the rotations cancel and the mixture is not optically active. Both ideas are needed for the mark: 'equal' and 'optical isomers / enantiomers'.

reasoningChain: Say the two optical isomers (enantiomers) are both present.
Say they are present in equal amounts.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing 'a mixture of optical isomers' without saying the amounts are equal.
Describing only the result (no rotation of polarised light) without saying what the mixture contains.

stem.text: Alanine has an isoelectric point of 6.11.
Explain what is meant by isoelectric point.

guidance: I ‘pH when the molecule has no charge’ alone.

points.text:
pH at (which a molecule / amino acid) has
and
no overall charge / is neutral / is a zwitterion [1]

explanation.text: The isoelectric point is the pH at which an amino acid carries no overall charge. At this pH almost all molecules exist as the zwitterion, <sup>+</sup>H<sub>3</sub>N–CH(R)–COO<sup>–</sup>, which has one positive and one negative charge. The word 'overall' (or 'zwitterion') matters: 'no charge' alone is ignored, because the zwitterion does carry charges.

reasoningChain: State that it is a pH value.
State that at this pH the amino acid has no overall charge (exists as a zwitterion).

inferredMistakes.text: Writing 'the pH when the molecule has no charge', which the MS ignores because the zwitterion has charges that cancel.

stem.text: Draw the structure of alanine at pH 10.

explanation.text: pH 10 is well above the isoelectric point of alanine (6.11), so the solution is alkaline. OH<sup>–</sup> removes H<sup>+</sup> from the –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group of the zwitterion, leaving a neutral –NH<sub>2</sub> group, while the carboxyl group stays as –COO<sup>–</sup>. The overall structure is the anion CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)COO<sup>–</sup>.

reasoningChain: Compare pH 10 with the isoelectric point 6.11: the solution is more alkaline.
In alkali, the amine group is not protonated (–NH₂) and the acid group is deprotonated (–COO⁻).

inferredMistakes.text: Drawing the zwitterion +H₃NCH(CH₃)COO⁻, which is the form at the isoelectric point, not at pH 10.
Drawing the cation +H₃NCH(CH₃)COOH, which is the form in acid.

stem.text: Alanine molecules can react together to form the tripeptide Ala–Ala–Ala.
Draw the structure for this tripeptide. The functional groups formed should be displayed.

guidance: A ecf for 1 mark here for M2 – repeat error. [The MS shows a scanned example: a displayed tripeptide drawn with the same error in each residue, annotated ECF with a tick and a cross.]
Also ecf M2 if H omitted on both N – repeat error.
A M1 if more than 2 amide links but M2 not available.

points.text:
M1 two peptide linkage shown
(C=O needs to be displayed but allow NH not displayed)

M2 rest of the structure correct
DEP on M1 (except for specific ecfs in guidance)
A carboxylate ion / zwitterion / NH3+ ion

markScheme.note: The MS answer is a drawn structure; shown as ms.figure. A scanned example response in the Guidance column is described in words.

figure.alt: Skeletal structure of Ala–Ala–Ala: H2N–CH(CH3)–C(=O)–NH–CH(CH3)–C(=O)–NH–CH(CH3)–COOH, with both C=O groups and both N–H bonds drawn.

explanation.text: Each peptide (amide) bond forms when the –COOH of one alanine reacts with the –NH<sub>2</sub> of the next, losing H<sub>2</sub>O. Three alanines joined in a row give two peptide links: H<sub>2</sub>N–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–C(=O)–NH–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–C(=O)–NH–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–COOH. The chain has a free –NH<sub>2</sub> at one end and a free –COOH at the other, and each residue keeps its CH<sub>3</sub> side chain. 'Displayed' means the C=O of each peptide link must be drawn as a double bond (the N–H may be condensed).

reasoningChain: Join them with two displayed peptide links, –C(=O)–NH–.
Finish with H₂N– at one end and –COOH at the other.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing the peptide link backwards as –CO–HN– or in condensed form without a displayed C=O, which the MS marks as a contradiction for M1.
Drawing three peptide links (four residues) or leaving out a CH₃ side chain, which loses M2.

stem.text: Compound J can be synthesised from alanine in three steps, as shown in Figure 7.1.

stem.caption: Figure 7.1
stem.alt: Synthesis route: alanine (H2N–CH(CH3)–COOH) goes by step 1 to an empty box labelled G, C5H9NO3; step 2 leads down to an empty box labelled H, C5H8NO2Cl; step 3 leads to J, drawn as CH3–C(=O)–NH–CH(CH3)–C(=O)–C6H5 (a benzene ring attached to the ketone carbon).

stem.text: Draw the structures of compounds G and H in the boxes in Figure 7.1.

markScheme.note: The MS answer is two drawn structures labelled M1M2; shown as ms.figure.

figure.alt: Skeletal structures. G: CH3–C(=O)–NH–CH(CH3)–C(=O)OH. H: CH3–C(=O)–NH–CH(CH3)–C(=O)Cl.

explanation.text: Work backwards from J. J has a CH3C(=O)–NH– group on the nitrogen of alanine and a phenyl ketone, –C(=O)–C6H5, where alanine had COOH. The formulas confirm each step: alanine (C3H7NO2) gains C2H2O to give G, C5H9NO3, which is the amide CH3CONHCH(CH3)COOH. Replacing OH by Cl gives H, C5H8NO2Cl, the acyl chloride. H then acylates benzene (Friedel–Crafts) to give the ketone J.

reasoningChain: Compare alanine with J: the NH₂ has become an amide, the COOH has become a phenyl ketone.
Use G's formula C₅H₉NO₃: only the NH₂ has changed, so G = CH₃CONHCH(CH₃)COOH.
Use H's formula C₅H₈NO₂Cl: the OH of COOH is replaced by Cl, so H = CH₃CONHCH(CH₃)COCl.

inferredMistakes.text: Making the ester or acyl chloride at the COOH end first, giving a structure for G that does not fit C₅H₉NO₃.
Drawing H as a chloroalkane (Cl on carbon) instead of the acyl chloride –COCl.

stem.text: Suggest reagents and conditions for steps 1 to 3 in Figure 7.1.

guidance: ecf penalise (aq) once only in step 1,2 and 3.
A any viable halogen carrier for acylation (e.g. FeBr3).

points.text:
M1 step 1 CH3COCl CON (aq)
CON additional reagent e.g. AlCl3, cH2SO4

explanation.text: Step 1 makes an amide from the amine: ethanoyl chloride reacts with a primary amine at room temperature. Step 2 turns the carboxylic acid into an acyl chloride with PCl3 and heat, PCl5 or SOCl2. Step 3 is Friedel–Crafts acylation: the acyl chloride H reacts with benzene with AlCl3 (or another halogen carrier such as FeBr3) as catalyst.

None of these reagents can be aqueous: water hydrolyses acyl chlorides, PCl3, PCl5, SOCl2 and AlCl3. The MS penalises (aq) once only across the three steps. An extra catalyst in step 1 (AlCl3 or cH2SO4) contradicts, because amide formation needs no catalyst.

reasoningChain: Step 2: COOH → COCl with PCl₃ + heat, PCl₅ or SOCl₂.
Step 3: acylate benzene with C₆H₆ and AlCl₃.

inferredMistakes.text: Adding AlCl₃ or concentrated H₂SO₄ in step 1, which the MS marks as a contradiction.
Giving only 'AlCl₃' for step 3 without benzene, which is the other reactant that supplies the phenyl group.
